### Monte Carlo simulation

**Finish the exercise!!*

Imagine the distribution of tree heights in a forest. It follows a Gompertz distribution with
mean `mu = 10` and standard deviation `sigma = 2`. In an exercise I can give you this numbers
but in the real world you don't know them. So you need to estimate them.

Now, we cannot measure every tree in the forest so we will measure a random sample of them and
use the mean and standard deviation of the sample as estimates of the forest mean and standard
deviation. We know that these estimate are not exact and they will vary depending on the
actual sample of trees we draw. A fundamental question in statistics is to understand how
would these estimates vary across all possible random samples from the same forest.

The answer to that question is known because smart statisticians worked out the math
decades ago. But if I change the assumptions (e.g., the distribution of heights is not
normal), we will often end up without a mathematical result. Doing statistics when everything
is Normal and Linear is easy, but also very unrealistic as nature is not Normal and Linear.

How can we approximate these results

```r
n_sim = 1000              # number of simulated experiments
sample_size = 25          # observations per experiment

sample_means = numeric(n_sim)

for (i in 1:n_sim) {
  sample = rnorm(sample_size, mean = 10, sd = 2)
  sample_means[i] = mean(sample)
}

mean(sample_means)        # close to 10
sd(sample_means)          # close to 2 / sqrt(25) = 0.4
hist(sample_means)
```

This pattern — repeat a random experiment many times, store the result of each run, then
summarize — will appear several times in this course, as it is useful when dealing with
probability distributions and statistical inference.
